overview: Corpay is a global B2B payments and spend-management company, renamed from FleetCor Technologies (ticker changed FLT -> CPAY in 2024), that helps businesses pay vendors, employees and fleet-related expenses in a controlled, digital manner. It operates through three reportable segments -- Corporate Payments (AP automation, cross-border FX/payments, virtual and purchasing/T&E cards), Vehicle Payments (fuel cards, Brazilian electronic tolling, EV charging, vehicle compliance) and Lodging Payments (discounted corporate/airline/insurance hotel bookings) -- plus an Other bucket (gift cards, payroll cards, outsourced card processing). Roughly 76% of revenue comes from the U.S., Brazil and the U.K., and the company has grown overwhelmingly through more than 100 acquisitions since 2002.

business_model.summary: Corpay earns net revenue (interchange/spread, card fees, FX spreads on cross-border trades, late fees/finance charges and float income) on recurring, volume-driven B2B transaction flows rather than one-off project fees. Revenue scales with customer spend/transaction volume, so it behaves like a high-margin, asset-light payments network business with substantial pricing power in niches where it owns proprietary acceptance networks (e.g., Sem Parar tolling in Brazil, its virtual-card merchant network).

revenue_streams.name: Vehicle Payments (fuel cards, tolls/Sem Parar, EV charging, vehicle compliance)
revenue_streams.trend: stable, fuel-price sensitive, structurally pressured by EV transition

revenue_streams.name: Corporate Payments (AP automation, cross-border FX, virtual/purchasing cards)
revenue_streams.trend: growing fast via M&A (Alpha, GPS, Paymerang, AvidXchange stake) and organic cross-border volume

revenue_streams.name: Lodging Payments (workforce, airline crew, insurance housing)
Other (gift cards, payroll cards, outsourced card processing)

business_model.customer_type: Predominantly B2B -- businesses and public-sector fleets of all sizes (SMB to large enterprise), plus some consumer-facing products (Brazil fuel/toll/parking, UK EV charging) and financial-institution/partner white-label relationships
business_model.geographic_mix: United States ~44%, Brazil ~16%, United Kingdom ~15%, Other ~24% (nine months ended Sept 30, 2026); approximately 44-51% of revenue is non-USD denominated, concentrated in BRL, GBP, EUR, CAD, AUD, MXN, CZK, NZD

main_competitors: American Express (Global Business Travel and corporate cards)
AvidXchange (now a Corpay-affiliated minority investee via TPG JV)
emerging B2B spend fintechs (Bill.com, Ramp, Brex)
competitive_position.market_position: Top-two global fuel-card/fleet-payments provider (duopoly with WEX in much of North America), a leading electronic-tolling operator in Brazil (Sem Parar covers ~100% of Brazil's RFID-enabled toll roads), and a fast-growing but still fragmented player in cross-border B2B FX/AP automation following the 2025 Alpha Group and GPS Capital Markets acquisitions

moat_factors.description: Owns closed-loop networks (fuel-card acceptance, Sem Parar tolling, virtual-card merchant-enrollment network) that capture richer transaction data and better economics than open networks like Mastercard/Visa
Strong positions across four continents and multiple payment verticals provide a 'portfolio effect' that smooths results when one geography or business underperforms
ERP integrations, white-label platforms and multi-year partner/bank relationships (oil majors, leasing companies, Mastercard sponsor banks) create stickiness, though contracts are periodically re-bid

Long track record (100+ deals since 2002) of acquiring bolt-on payment businesses and cross-selling into the combined customer base, most recently Alpha, GPS, Paymerang, Gringo and a strategic stake in AvidXchange
Extensive money-transmitter and payment-instrument licensing across jurisdictions raises entry barriers for new competitors, though it also raises compliance costs

weaknesses: Legacy consumer-protection litigation (FTC) signals past weaknesses in sales/marketing practices that could resurface reputationally
Heavy reliance on serial M&A increases integration risk and makes organic performance harder to assess
Fuel card economics (still ~43% of revenue) face long-term secular pressure from EV adoption and fuel price/spread volatility
Elevated leverage after debt-funded Alpha acquisition and aggressive buybacks
Past material weakness in IT general/user-access controls (FY2023-FY2024) raised control-environment concerns, even though remediated by FY2025
Significant emerging-market (Brazil) and FX exposure introduces earnings volatility outside management's control

growth_drivers: Corporate Payments buildout via M&A: Alpha Group ($2.4B, closed Oct 2025) extends B2B cross-border FX/alternative banking into Europe with plans to expand into the US and Asia; GPS Capital Markets and Paymerang add treasury/cross-border and AP automation capabilities

Strategic stake in AvidXchange (35% via TPG joint venture, with a call option to acquire the rest at ~2.5x invested capital after 33 months) gives an inside track into a larger lower/middle-market AP automation platform
Continued expansion of Mastercard partnership (2.3% equity stake sold to Mastercard for $300M) to broaden cross-border payment distribution
Spend-management platform build-out with AI-enabled analytics, anomaly detection and policy-compliance tools layered onto virtual card/AP data
EV charging network expansion in the U.S., U.K. and Europe to capture 'mixed fleet' transaction economics as fleets electrify
Stablecoin/blockchain integration in the cross-border business to defend against disintermediation

Portfolio pruning (PayByPhone sold March 2026 for ~$425M net; UK Maintenance business sold for ~£600M/~$800M, closed Nov 2026; BP private-label fuel card portfolio sold) is recycling capital from lower-growth/non-core assets into higher-growth Corporate Payments M&A and buybacks
Large, continuing share-repurchase program (~$1.8B repurchased in the first nine months of 2026) supporting EPS growth

business.description: WEX, American Express, Coupa, banks and newer fintechs (Ramp, Bill.com) compete on price, network acceptance and bundled offerings; large competitors can bundle treasury/lending products
Fuel-linked revenue (~43% of total) is exposed to retail fuel price and price-spread swings and to the long-term shift toward electric vehicles, which changes unit economics
Relies on relationships with oil majors, Mastercard sponsor banks, leasing companies and airlines; loss of key relationships or unfavorable re-bids could hurt revenue
Extends trade credit to a wide range of business customers and bears counterparty credit risk on cross-border derivative contracts; a downturn could raise bad-debt expense
Vehicle Payments revenue is weaker in Q1/Q4 (weather, Brazil summer/Carnival) and gift-card revenue is concentrated in Q3/Q4 holiday season

financial.description: Total debt rose to ~$11.2B at Sept 30, 2026 (from ~$10.0B at year-end 2025) after the Alpha acquisition and credit-facility upsizing, alongside ~$1.8B of share buybacks in the first nine months of 2026
44-51% of revenue is non-USD (heavily Brazilian real, GBP, EUR); results and reported growth are sensitive to currency translation and to cross-currency swap settlement outcomes
Cross-border FX business carries ~$170B of notional customer derivative contracts; counterparty default or collateral-call liquidity strain is a recurring disclosed risk

TPG/AvidXchange partnership carries a minimum-return guarantee of up to 1.6x invested capital under certain exit scenarios, and Mastercard holds a put right (2027-2028) on its cross-border stake at invested capital plus 8% compounded

regulatory.description: FTC v. FleetCor (filed 2019) alleged unfair/deceptive marketing practices in the U.S. direct fuel-card business; after an adverse Eleventh Circuit ruling (Jan 2026) and denied en banc review (May 2026), the company recorded a $100M charge in Q3 2026 under a proposed consent order still awaiting FTC Commissioner and District Court approval -- final terms or additional redress/penalties could change
Operates under extensive U.S. state and foreign money-transmitter/payment-instrument licensing regimes subject to periodic examinations and potential findings
Mastercard interchange fees and late-fee/finance-charge revenue (together a meaningful revenue share) are subject to regulatory and legislative scrutiny that could cap pricing
Evolving, inconsistent rules on stablecoins and blockchain payments could impose new licensing or operational burdens as Corpay integrates these capabilities into cross-border solutions

macro.description: Tariffs, sanctions, and conflicts (Ukraine, Middle East) could affect cross-border payment volumes, bank relationships and compliance costs
Material variable-rate debt (partially hedged via $2.5B notional SOFR swaps) means rising rates increase interest expense net of hedges
B2B transaction volumes, fleet activity and corporate travel/lodging spend are cyclical and would contract in a broad economic downturn

execution.description: Simultaneous integration of Alpha ($2.4B), the AvidXchange/TPG partnership, GPS Capital Markets, Paymerang and Gringo, alongside divestitures of PayByPhone and the UK Maintenance business and a Q1 2026 segment realignment, creates significant near-term integration and reporting-comparability risk

A material weakness in IT general/user-access controls was disclosed for FY2023-FY2024 (adverse ICFR opinion for FY2024); the FY2025 10-K reflects an unqualified, effective ICFR opinion (excluding the 2025 Gringo/Alpha acquisitions from scope), indicating remediation but warranting continued monitoring
CFO Tom Panther departed in March 2025 and was replaced by Peter Walker; CEO Ronald Clarke (since 2000) remains Chairman/CEO with no announced succession plan

macro_factors.industry_outlook: B2B payments digitization remains a large, early-stage secular opportunity (management estimates ~$145 trillion of annual B2B spend, much of it still paper/manual), supporting continued double-digit growth in AP automation and cross-border FX even as the legacy fuel-card category matures and faces EV-driven disruption
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate -- revenue is transaction/spend-volume-linked and correlates with business activity, fuel prices and corporate travel, but the diversified segment and geographic mix smooths volatility
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate -- sizeable variable-rate term loan and revolver balances (partially hedged with ~$2.5B notional interest-rate swaps) mean financing costs move with SOFR; also benefits from interest income on customer float/collateral balances
key_input_costs: Retail fuel prices and fuel price spreads (~6-8% of revenue tied directly to fuel price levels)
Interchange/network fees paid on Mastercard-branded transactions
Foreign exchange rates affecting translated non-USD revenue (~44-51% of total)

recent_developments.event: Completed acquisition of Alpha Group International plc for approximately £1.8 billion ($2.4 billion), expanding B2B cross-border FX and alternative banking capability in the UK/Europe; funded via upsized credit facility

Closed formation of a TPG-led limited partnership that acquired AvidXchange Holdings; Corpay invested ~$578 million for ~35% of the JV (enterprise value ~$1.9 billion) with a call right to acquire the rest after 33 months
Mastercard's $300 million investment for a 2.3% stake in Corpay's cross-border payments business closed, with reciprocal put/call rights in 2027-2028
Closed divestiture of the BP private-label fuel card portfolio for approximately $60 million
Sold PayByPhone, the mobile parking payments business within Vehicle Payments, for total proceeds of ~$424.7 million net of cash, recording a $125.5 million pre-tax gain
Refined segment composition (realigned outsourced card processing into 'Other' and spend-management enterprise clients into Corporate Payments); prior periods recast
Signed a definitive agreement to sell the UK Maintenance business for approximately £600 million (~$800 million); classified as held for sale and completed November 2, 2026

Reached a proposed consent order with FTC staff to resolve the long-running FleetCor marketing-practices litigation, recording a $100 million legal settlement charge, pending FTC Commissioner and District Court approval
Reported Q3 2026 adjusted EPS of $7.54 (vs. ~$7.19-$7.20 consensus) on revenue of $1.38 billion (+18% YoY); raised full-year 2026 guidance; shares rose roughly 10% on the print
Amended Credit Agreement (18th amendment, May 2026) to upsize the revolver to $3.7B and Term Loan A to $3.3B and extend maturities to 2031, alongside a $2.95B Term Loan B-6 maturing 2032

items.notes: Implies continued double-digit growth over FY2025 revenue of $4.53 billion, driven by Alpha/AvidXchange contribution and organic Corporate Payments growth
Up from prior guidance of $27.15 - $27.55; follows a Q3 beat of $7.54 adjusted EPS vs. ~$7.19-$7.20 consensus
Nine-month 2026 adjusted EBITDA margin was 56.5%, consistent with the prior-year period; Q3 2026 margin was 57.4%
Management indicated expected organic revenue growth of 9-11% for 2027 on the Q3 2026 earnings call

guidance.management_commentary: CFO Peter Walker attributed the Corporate Payments acceleration to spend management and cross-border FX activity and highlighted 57.4% Q3 EBITDA margins from high revenue flow-through. Management cautioned that an approximately 100-basis-point benefit to Q3 margins/revenue from customer-fund monetization may not recur in Q4 2026. CEO Ronald Clarke continues to frame the business around a 'compounding growth model' combining organic cross-sell with M&A, most recently Alpha and the AvidXchange stake.

bull_case: Corporate Payments (now ~41% of revenue) is compounding at 30-40%+ reported growth, re-rating the business toward a software/payments-platform multiple as the legacy fuel-card mix shrinks as a share of the total
Large, underpenetrated B2B payments TAM (~$145 trillion of estimated global B2B spend) still largely manual, giving a long runway for AP automation and cross-border FX adoption

Disciplined portfolio recycling -- divesting lower-growth/non-core assets (PayByPhone, UK Maintenance, BP portfolio) and redeploying into higher-growth Corporate Payments M&A (Alpha, AvidXchange, GPS) and heavy buybacks (~$1.8B in 9M 2026)
FTC litigation overhang, pending since 2017-2019, is largely resolved with a capped $100 million charge, removing a long-standing legal uncertainty
Internal-control material weakness from FY2023-FY2024 has been remediated, with an unqualified ICFR opinion issued for FY2025, reducing governance risk
Strong free cash flow and EBITDA margins (~56-57%) support continued aggressive capital return alongside M&A
bear_case: Leverage has risen meaningfully (total debt ~$11.2B vs. ~$3.3B of equity at Sept 30, 2026) after the debt-funded Alpha acquisition and continued large buybacks, reducing financial flexibility

Heavy, continuous M&A activity (Alpha, AvidXchange/TPG, GPS, Paymerang, Gringo) alongside simultaneous divestitures and a segment realignment makes organic performance difficult to assess and raises integration-execution risk
Vehicle Payments (still ~43% of revenue) remains exposed to fuel price/spread volatility and the secular EV transition, a structural headwind to the largest legacy segment
FTC consent order is not yet finally approved; terms could change, and the episode highlights historical sales-practice risk that could resurface or invite further regulatory scrutiny
Significant non-USD revenue exposure (44-51%), concentrated in Brazilian real and British pound, creates earnings volatility outside of operational control
Complex contingent obligations (TPG/AvidXchange minimum-return guarantee up to 1.6x invested capital, Mastercard put option in 2027) could require unplanned cash outlays
